entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text:
I don't need a monitor after all: the background A/B will notify me when it exits.

So far:
- **The flash tool had a bug.** It built each image, then flashed with different build flags, so PlatformIO cleaned the build and deleted the image. Fixed and committed as `6ef7c1b` on `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`.
- **The first device profile is in:** Gears (light layout) runs at 13.8 fps, with a 61 ms step. It breaks down as:
  - Filling triangles: about 28 ms.
  - Transforming vertices, outside lighting: about 17 ms, or roughly 4 µs a vertex, which seems high for the maths involved.
  - Clear: about 5 ms.
  - Lighting: only about 3.7 ms.
- **What that means:** lazy shading can save at most about 2 ms on this layout. Fill and the per-vertex overhead are where the time goes.
- **In progress:** a 5-way A/B on Gears, two rounds of 60 s each, about 15 minutes. It compares a profile-only baseline against lazy shading, `GL_IRAM`, `GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES` and `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1`.

When it finishes I'll post the table, then profile CubicGrid and Morph3D.

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and its
  `assert()` aborts on a failed allocation, and it ran at 1.2 fps, so it is
  shelved (issue #37): its source stays in `firmware/src/hacks/celtic/`, it is
  not in `g_hacks[]`, and `failed_ports.txt` lists it. A failed port that has
  its source and a measured row still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed
  standalone. Measure on the device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.

I've rerun the A/B, because the first attempt never flashed anything. The tool had a second flaw: building the next variant changed the build flags, so PlatformIO cleaned the shared build directory and deleted the earlier image. With a single variant the problem didn't show.

Each variant now gets its own build directory. That fix is committed as `c63aed1`, after the first fix `6ef7c1b`.

The run compares five variants on Gears, all with profiling on:

- profiling alone
- lazy shading
- `GL_IRAM`
- `GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES`
- `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1`

Each variant now builds from scratch, then gets two rounds of 60 seconds on the board, so it'll take a while. I'll post the table when it finishes.

lines: /* Issue #43 experiment: the data cache's hardware next-line prefetch

+ * board boot-looped. It runs from the canvas (allocated first) to the end of

# GL budget: cubicgrid and morph3d

`tools/gl_budget.py` runs a GL hack on the host, counts what each frame asks of
TinyGL, and predicts the device frame time. It was built to choose between two
candidates for the next GL port (issue #45) without flashing either.

```text
uv run tools/gl_budget.py [--frames N] [--seeds a,b,c]
    [--override '*name: value' ...] name[:seed] ...
```

Gears is read from `firmware/src/hacks/gears/`; any other name from
`vendor/xscreensaver-6.16/hacks/glx/` (git-ignored, never copied into the
repo). A hack that does not build is reported with its first error, and the
exit status is 1.

`--override` gives the hack a resource line that beats its own defaults, as an
entry in `registry.c`'s override list does on the device. Repeat it for more.
It applies to every hack named, so run hacks with different overrides
separately. Use it to try a registry override (`--override '*count: 40'`)
before committing to it, or to supply one a hack needs to start.

## What it counts

The counters sit inside a private copy of TinyGL, built only for the tool
(`firmware/src/tinygl/` and the firmware builds are untouched). Counting there
means a display list that is built once and replayed every frame is counted on
every frame. Per frame, it records:

- **Vertices** set up, and how many of them were lit.
- **Triangles** rasterised, after back-face culling, and the **pixels** they

- **Lines** and **points** drawn.

content.text:
Rod, the board measurements are in. In short: **lazy shading is a real, modest gain, and the main cost is PSRAM cache misses, not arithmetic.**

**Lazy shading A/B** (two rounds each, frame times repeat to within 0.05 ms):

| Hack | Profile only | `GL_LAZY_SHADE` | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gears (light layout) | 61.1 ms, 13.8 fps | 57.7 ms, 14.5 fps | −3.4 ms |
| Morph3D | 61.4 ms, 13.9 fps | 58.4 ms, 14.4 fps | −3.0 ms |
| CubicGrid (points, unlit) | 47.9 ms | 47.9 ms | none, as expected |

**The memory flags barely help** (Gears):
- **`GL_IRAM`:** 0.7 ms slower.
- **`GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES`:** no change.
- **`PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1`:** no change.
- **`PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=3`:** 0.8 ms faster.
- **A boot loop, now fixed:** my first autoload build boot-looped the board. Its prefetch region covered unmapped addresses, so the panic handler itself crashed and the watchdog reset the board. It now prefetches over mapped PSRAM only. The boot loop ended with the next flash.

**Where Gears' frame goes:**
- **Fill:** 28 ms, about 47% of the frame.
- **Vertex transform, excluding lighting:** about 17 ms, roughly 4 µs a vertex.
- **Clear:** 6 ms.
- **Lighting:** only 3.7 ms, which is why lazy shading can't save more.

**Why fill is slow:** I added a boot-time benchmark to `GL_PROFILE` builds. Each access to a new PSRAM cache line costs 129 cycles to read, and about 220 if the line is then written. Gears' triangles average about 30 pixels, and every row touches new lines in both the z-buffer and the canvas. That accounts for roughly 23 of the 28 ms. CubicGrid's scattered points cost about 350 cycles each, for the same reason.

The Arduino SDK is fixed at a 32 KB data cache with 32-byte lines, and PSRAM at 80 MHz. The chip can do a 64 KB cache and 64-byte lines, but only with a rebuilt SDK.

**On the branch** (`feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`, pushed):
- **`ab_flash.py` fixes:** each variant now gets its own build directory. Before, PlatformIO deleted the previous image whenever the flags changed.
- **The autoload fix.**
- **The benchmark.**

The board is on a pinned CubicGrid build with profiling and lazy shading on, and rotation off.

**Decisions for you:**
1. **Make `GL_LAZY_SHADE` the default?** It's exact on the host and about 5% faster on the board. Every GL hack would see the change, so it needs your yes.
2. **Biggest remaining lever: render in bands in internal RAM.** Transform once, sort triangles into horizontal bands, rasterise each band against a z-buffer and colour band held in internal RAM, then copy the band out. That could cut fill and clear from about 34 ms to under 10 on Gears, but it means reworking how TinyGL rasterises. I'd want to design it with you before I start.
3. **Post these numbers on #43, and update the overnight report?** Your earlier approval for issue comments covered the overnight work, so I'm asking again.
4. **Reflash the board with `main`'s normal rotating build when we're done?**

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `gh pr merge N --merge` once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). His approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire
  Gates check to finish. A stacked PR's gate
  can fail "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges: if approvals
  and findings pass and the PR is mergeable, merge it, with no rebase.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- `entire agent-help` says trails are unavailable; `entire trail create` works.
  Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md` (rows, paragraphs and
  the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.

out the `GL_LINE_LOOP` case in `glopVertex`. Such a primitive falls through to
`default:`, which draws nothing but leaves the vertex count climbing. The fifth
vertex writes past `c->vertex[POLYGON_MAX_VERTEX]` into the GL context after
it (the inverse modelview, the projection, the current colours). Pipes'
`buildlwo.c` draws `GL_POLYGON`s and crashed the host on frame 16 this way.

## The fix

- `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the `default:` case sets `n = 0`, so an unhandled
  primitive keeps reusing the first slot. TinyGL itself stays byte-identical.
- `test_glshim`: a test draws a 12-vertex `GL_POLYGON` and checks the
  projection matrix and current colour come through untouched. It fails
  without the patch.
- `.claude/rules/gl.md`: a gotcha saying `GL_POLYGON` and `GL_LINE_LOOP` draw
  nothing on this build.

No pixels change: these primitives drew nothing before either. That means
StonerView's square outlines and Unknown Pleasures' rim loop have never been
drawn on the board. Turning `GL_POLYGON` on to draw them would change how those
hacks look, so it's left out of this PR.

## Verified

- Host tests: 557 of 557 pass, and 344 Python tests, on a trial merge with
  current `main` (the branch predates batch 3).
- Not flashed: the change only affects primitives no registered hack draws
  successfully.

entries.name: EnterWorktree
entries.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

name.description: Optional name for a new worktree. Each "/"-separated segment may contain only letters, digits, dots, underscores, and dashes; max 64 chars total. A random name is generated if not provided. Mutually exclusive with `path`.

path.description: Path to an existing worktree to switch into instead of creating a new one. Must appear in `git worktree list` for the current repo — or, on first entry from the launch directory, for a repo nested inside it (multi-repo workspace). Mutually exclusive with `name`.

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

Done so far:
- **Primitive fix:** draft PR #79 is open: https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/pull/79. A trial merge with current `main` passed 557/557 host tests and 344 Python tests.
- **Lazy shading:** it's now the default on the experiments branch. `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` turns it back off. There's a new test that failed before the change and passes after. The GL tests pass under every flag combination.
- **Still running:** the full suite, which checks every frame hash is unchanged. Once it's green I'll commit, post the numbers on #43 and update the report. I'll reflash the board with `main`'s rotating build at the end, so the experiments can keep using it until then.

On the banded renderer: if you'd rather skip the questions and have me write the design straight away, just say so.

Otherwise: when you picture this working, which hacks do you most want faster, and what frame rate would make this much rework worth it to you?

off. All 520 host tests pass, and every pinned frame hash is unchanged.

- `GL_IRAM`: 0.7 ms slower.
- `GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES`: no change.
- `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1` (prefetch on a miss): no change. `=3` (hit and miss):
  0.8 ms faster.

content.content:
Issues #43 and #44 · night of 10 to 11 October 2026

TinyGL overnight report

Rod, here is what I tried on GL speed and Pipes while you slept, what I learned, and what I'd like to flash first. Nothing has touched the board: every number here is from the host or from the device build, and the board estimates are labelled as estimates.

The short version

Best lead

Lazy lighting (GL_LAZY_SHADE): TinyGL lights every vertex before back-face culling throws most of them away. Lighting only what gets drawn halves the lighting work in Gears' heavy layout, and every frame hash is identical.

Tool

One-flash profile (GL_PROFILE): cycle counts per stage printed next to each run line, so a single capture gives the whole breakdown instead of one flash per early return.

Pipes

An exact incremental redraw works on the host (about 300 vertices a frame instead of up to 977,000). But Pipes as written needs about 22 MB of display lists, and the board has about 7 MB free. It can fit with smaller screens and a fixed camera.

Bug

TinyGL here draws no GL_LINE_LOOPs, so StonerView's square outlines have never shown, and a loop or polygon of more than four vertices overwrote the GL context. I fixed the overwrite; whether to draw the outlines is your call.

What I learned about where the time goes

  • It isn't soft-float any more. I disassembled the device build. The vertex and triangle path calls only ROM __divsf3 (a 48-byte FPU routine) and newlib sqrtf. Software double shows up only on the specular and positional-light paths, which no ported hack uses. GCC 8.4 won't inline sqrtf or a divide, even with -fno-math-errno.
  • The hot code is small. A per-frame call profile on the host, mapped onto the device function sizes, comes to about 6 KB of code for Gears' heavy layout and 3 KB for CubicGrid. The instruction cache is 16 KB, so flash-cache misses are probably not the main cost.
  • The data side is the likelier suspect. Display lists are PSRAM reads of 20 to 52 bytes a vertex (a glColor op alone is 32 bytes), and the z-buffer and canvas are PSRAM too, behind a 32 KB data cache with 32-byte lines. The lists can't move to internal RAM: Gears' heavy layout reads about 420 KB of list ops a frame.
  • Culling discards most of the lighting. Gears' heavy layout submits 17,624 triangles and fills 5,330, but lights all 17,700 vertices first. That is what lazy lighting goes after.
----

What I'd like to flash, in order

  1. GL_PROFILE alone, pinned to Gears (first layout), then CubicGrid. One capture each gives the stage breakdown that everything else should be judged against.
  2. Lazy lighting A/B on Gears and Morph3D. If the board agrees with the host, I'd propose it as the default.
  3. GL_IRAM, GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES, PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1, one at a time, keeping only what moves step.
  4. Then, depending on the profile, the bigger moves: running the panel flush on core 0 while the next frame starts (it reads M5GFX's buffer, not the canvas, but releasing the SPI bus from another task needs care), or rasterising on core 0 while core 1 transforms.
.venv/bin/python -I tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 \
    --out /tmp/ab --keys fps,step,push,list,vertex,shade,tri,fill \
    "prof=-DGL_PROFILE" "lazy=-DGL_PROFILE -DGL_LAZY_SHADE"

Decisions for you

  1. Permission to flash for the measurements above (the board still holds whatever the last session left).
  2. Draw line loops (GL_POLYGON on), changing StonerView and Unknown Pleasures, or keep today's look.
  3. For Pipes: a fixed camera, smaller screens, what to do about the fade, and building the unlicensed helpers from vendor/.
  4. Whether GL_PROFILE and ab_flash.py should land on main as tools.

Where it all is

  • Branches (pushed, no PRs): feature/43-gl-speed-experiments, feature/44-pipes, fix/tinygl-unhandled-primitive.
  • Comments: #43 and #44.
  • Not done: nothing flashed or measured on the board; no PRs opened; the Pipes port itself (it's waiting on the decisions above); gl_budget.py still counts every lit vertex, so it will over-predict once lazy lighting is on.

Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Goop/Loop/Starfish/Qix/Hypnowheel/FireworkX batch.

## What

Hypnowheel is ported and renders correctly but runs at 1.4 fps on the device
(step 720 ms), far under the 15 fps bar. Nothing in the hack's own settings
fixes it.

## What was measured

| Build | fps | step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered (4 layers, 13 arms) | 1.4 | 720 ms |
| `*layers: 1` | 4.4 | 200 ms |
| `*count: 5` (about 7x fewer triangles, same area) | 2.0 | 511 ms |

The probes were temporary registry overrides, since reverted. From them, about
70 percent of the step is additively blended pixel fill (435k pixels at about
1.2 us each) and about 30 percent is per-triangle setup (about 35 us each, 5,900
triangles). `tools/gl_budget.py` predicted 359 ms; it understates blended fill
by about 2x here.

## Ideas, not tried

- A faster `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` span in the patched TinyGL (the canvas pixels are
  RGB565, so a saturating add can be done two pixels at a time with masks).
- Render the GL framebuffer at half the width and height and upscale in
  `glshim`, as `hacks/lowrez_put.h` does for Fireworkx (a quarter of the
  pixels). Both change shared GL code, so they need Rod's say-so.

Code: `firmware/src/hacks/hypnowheel/`, `hypnowheel_gl.c`.

content.text:
Both are in the numbers already, and they point the same way as Gears, only harder.

**What I know so far:**
- **Hypnowheel** runs at 1.4 fps (720 ms a frame). It was dropped from the rotation (#73).
  - **Blended fill, about 70%:** about 435,000 additively blended pixels a frame at about 1.2 µs each. That's roughly 290 cycles a pixel, and every one is a read-modify-write of the canvas in PSRAM.
  - **Triangle setup, about 30%:** about 5,900 triangles at about 35 µs each. My guess is that a fair share of that is PSRAM misses too.
- **Unknown Pleasures** runs at about 5 fps (about 165 ms a frame). It draws filled quads plus smoothed lines, with the depth test and polygon offset. I don't yet have a stage breakdown for it.

**My guess at what banding would buy:**
- **Hypnowheel:** with the blend done in internal RAM, at a few tens of cycles a pixel instead of about 290, it might go from 720 ms to somewhere around 150 to 250 ms. That's 4 to 6 fps: much better, but still nowhere near 15.
- **Unknown Pleasures:** probably a similar proportional gain, but I'd want its profile before guessing a number.

The design differs for these two. Big blended triangles span many bands, and blending needs the existing canvas pixels in each band, not just a cleared one.

I'd like to measure both on the board before designing:
1. Merge current `main` into the experiments branch.
2. Flash a `GL_PROFILE` build pinned to Unknown Pleasures.
3. Flash one pinned to Hypnowheel, registered only in that temporary build.

That gives a stage-by-stage breakdown for each, and a measured cost of a blended pixel against an opaque one.

Shall I go and profile them?

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. Other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.

content.text:
Here's what the board says about your three, and what it means for the design.

| Hack | Now | Where the time goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown Pleasures | 4.7 fps, 174 ms step | fill 69 ms, triangle setup 40 ms, smooth lines 30 ms, clear 25 ms; push 32 ms + 11 ms sync |
| Hypnowheel | 1.4 fps, 706 ms step | fill 358 ms, setup 61 ms, clear 12 ms, **about 275 ms in the hack's own `double` trig** |
| Pipes (host lab only) | not on the board | vertices and lighting, not fill |

**What that means:**
- **Hypnowheel has a cheap first win that isn't GL at all.** A single-precision wrapper, the same trick as Galaxy and Substrate with the hack left byte-identical, should take out most of the 275 ms. That's my estimate; I haven't built it yet.
- **Banding is aimed at fill, clear and lines.** That's about 165 ms of Unknown Pleasures' 174 ms and about 370 ms of Hypnowheel's. If rasterising in internal RAM costs a quarter of what it does in PSRAM, my guess is:
  - Unknown Pleasures: 174 → roughly 80 ms (about 9 fps with the push).
  - Hypnowheel: after the trig fix, roughly 150 ms (about 5 fps).
- **Pipes wants something different.** With a fixed camera, the incremental redraw already makes steady frames tiny; the fade is vertex-bound, which lazy lighting helps.
- **One clash to design around:** the incremental redraw needs the full z-buffer and canvas kept from the last frame. A banded renderer with z-buffer bands in internal RAM throws those away, so Pipes would either stay on the normal path or bands would have to be saved back.

So my guess is this is really three pieces of work:
1. Hypnowheel's trig.
2. The banded renderer, for Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel.
3. A Pipes port using the incremental redraw.

The banded renderer is the only big one.

What's wrong or missing in that? And for the banded renderer: must frames come out pixel-identical to today's, so every pinned frame hash still matches, or would you accept small differences for speed?

content.text:
#73 has no comments, but its body offers two ideas. Both fit now that pixel-identical isn't required:

1. **A faster additive blend.** The canvas is RGB565, so a saturating add can do two pixels at once with bit masks, instead of TinyGL's per-pixel decode and re-encode. That suits Hypnowheel's `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` fill.
2. **Render at half resolution and scale up**, as Fireworkx already does through `lowrez_put.h`. That's a quarter of the pixels.

There's a bonus with the second: at 233×233 the z-buffer is 108 KB, which might fit in internal RAM whole, with no bands needed. It would soften edges, though. That's fine for Hypnowheel's broad spirals, but I'd expect it to spoil Unknown Pleasures, whose look is its thin smoothed lines.

**My play-back of the design so far:**
- **Goal:** make Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel much faster. Pipes is a separate piece of work, built on the incremental redraw.
- **Exactness:** not required, so the pinned frame hashes can be re-pinned. I'd still want a test that compares banded frames with today's and fails on large differences.
- **Mechanism:**
  1. Transform each vertex once.
  2. Sort the screen-space triangles and lines into horizontal bands.
  3. Rasterise each band against a z-buffer and colour band in internal RAM.
  4. Copy each finished band out to the canvas.
  - Clearing becomes nearly free, because each band starts as the clear colour in fast memory.
- **Riding along in the same fast inner loop, my additions:** the two-pixel blend from #73 and quicker smooth lines.
- **Separate and first:** Hypnowheel's single-precision wrapper, since it's unrelated to rendering and cheap.
- **Half resolution:** kept as a per-hack option. My guess is it's for Hypnowheel only, and it needs your eye on the look.

content.text:
Not for the hacks we have. Every registered GL hack clears the screen each frame, and none uses textures or reads pixels back, so all of them fit the banded model cleanly. The downsides are real, but they all have the same answer, an automatic fallback:

1. **Frames that build on the last one.** A band starts life in fast memory as the clear colour. A frame that doesn't begin with a clear, like Pipes' incremental redraw, would need each band loaded from the PSRAM canvas and z-buffer and written back. That's slower than today's direct path. The renderer can see whether a frame started with a clear and draw directly when it didn't.
2. **Very large frames.** Every triangle is held until the frame ends, so the holding area needs a cap: Pipes' fade alone is about 977,000 vertices. If a frame overflows it, the renderer has to fall back for the rest of that frame, or flush part-way.
3. **Mid-frame state changes.** Each held triangle has to remember the blend mode, depth test, polygon offset and shading in force when it was drawn. That's more memory and more code to get right. Unknown Pleasures switches between filled quads and lines with an offset within one frame, so this matters from day one.
4. **Internal RAM.** Bands plus the holding area might want 60 to 120 KB of the roughly 305 KB free. Today that's fine, but it's taken from every hack, GL or not, unless it's only allocated while a GL hack runs. I'd allocate it only then.
5. **Simple scenes gain little.** CubicGrid's points and Morph3D's small object would pay the sorting cost for a small saving. I'd guess they still come out about even or ahead.
6. **One bug hits every GL hack at once.** It's mitigated by the frame comparison tests, but a bug would show everywhere rather than in one hack.

The upside of one path is a single thing to test and maintain, and every GL hack, including future ports, gets faster without anyone deciding per hack.

So my recommendation: one path, falling back to today's direct drawing for frames that don't start with a clear and for frames that overflow. That keeps Pipes' incremental redraw working unchanged.

Does one path with that automatic fallback sound right to you?

Good. Here's the play-back of how it would behave, with my calls marked as mine:

- **When:** a frame that starts with `glClear` of colour and depth is held. Every triangle, line and point is transformed and lit as now, then stored with its screen position, colours, depth, and the state in force at the time (blend, depth test, offset, shading).

- **Inner loops (my call):** the faster two-pixel additive blend from #73, and smooth lines that write to the band.
- **Separately, first:** Hypnowheel's single-precision wrapper.

input.content:
# Banded GL renderer: design

Issue #43. Agreed with Rod on 2026-10-11. This document is a planning
artefact: it lives on the feature branch and does not merge to `main`.

## Why

Rod wants Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel to run visibly faster on the
StopWatch. Hypnowheel was dropped from the rotation at 1.4 fps (issue #73).
Success is judged by Rod watching the board ("I know it when I see it"), not
by an fps target, so the work must stop at points where he can look.

Board profiles (`GL_PROFILE` builds of `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`,
pinned, rotation off; stage times nest):

| Hack | Step | Fill | Triangle setup outside fill | Lines | Clear | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown Pleasures | 174 ms | 69 ms (5,442 tris) | 40 ms | 30 ms (3,960) | 25 ms | push 32 ms + 11 ms sync |
| Hypnowheel | 706 ms | 358 ms (5,949 tris) | 61 ms | 0 | 12 ms | about 275 ms in the hack's `double` trig |
| Gears (boot layout) | 58 ms with lazy lighting | 28 ms (1,600 tris) | 2 ms | 0 | 6 ms | vertex work about 17 ms |

The cause of slow fill is PSRAM. A boot benchmark measured a new 32-byte PSRAM
cache line at 129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back, against
17 for internal RAM. Lines a row apart cost the same as lines in address
order, so hardware prefetch cannot help (measured: `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD` changed
Gears by under 1 ms). A small triangle touches new z-buffer and canvas lines on
every row. The Arduino SDK fixes the data cache at 32 KB with 32-byte lines.

The fix is to rasterise into internal RAM: hold a frame's primitives, then
draw the screen in horizontal bands whose colour and depth live in internal
RAM, copying each finished band to the canvas.

## Goals

- Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel visibly faster on the board, with Rod
  looking at each step.
- One rendering path for every GL hack, with an automatic fallback (below).
  No per-hack flag decides whether a hack is banded.
- Every registered GL hack keeps working and looks the same to the eye:
  Gears, Morph3D, CubicGrid, StonerView, Unknown Pleasures, HexTrail.

## Non-goals

- Pixel-identical output. Rod accepts small differences, so the pinned frame
  hashes in `test_hacks.c` will be re-pinned.
- Pipes. It is a separate piece of work built on the incremental redraw in
  `docs/pipes-lab/` (branch `feature/44-pipes`). This design must not break
  that redraw, and the fallback is what protects it.
- Vertex and lighting cost. Lazy lighting already landed on the experiments
  branch; per-vertex work is left alone here.
- Moving the push to the other core, a 64 KB data cache, or a faster PSRAM
  clock.

## Anti-goals

- A slower frame for any registered GL hack. The fallback exists so that
  frames the banded path cannot help draw as they do today.
- Taking internal RAM from non-GL hacks. Band memory is allocated only while
  a GL hack runs.
- Editing copied hacks. They stay byte-identical (AGENTS.md).

## Constraints

- ESP32-S3, 240 MHz. About 305 KB of internal heap is free while a GL hack
  runs (`heap=` in the `run` line). Canvas, z-buffer and display lists are in
  PSRAM (about 6 MB free).
- The canvas is 466 by 466 RGB565 with bytes swapped (display order). TinyGL
  draws straight into `canvas->px`, and the z-buffer is 16-bit.
- TinyGL under `firmware/src/tinygl/` stays byte-identical. All changes go
  through `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (checked anchors) or `firmware/src/glshim/`.
- The dirty-rectangle contract (`.claude/rules/gl.md`): TinyGL reports the box
  around what it draws to `glshim_note_box`, `glClear` clears only the box
  drawn since the last clear, and a swap marks only what was drawn and erased.
  Nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs.
- Behaviour already patched into TinyGL must survive banding: polygon offset
  with its snapping margin, smooth (Wu) lines with fractional endpoints,
  `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` treated as opaque, additive blending, the
  depth clear skipped while the depth test is off, and lazy lighting.
- Host tests first, under AddressSanitizer; mutation-check new tests.
- Rod has given standing permission to flash for this session. Report
  "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately.

## Decided

### Order of work

1. **Hypnowheel's trig, first and separately.** A single-precision wrapper for
   Hypnowheel, like Galaxy and Substrate (`.claude/skills/port-hack/`,
   "Single precision"). The hack stays byte-identical. Profile it on the board,
   which needs a temporary registry entry, as Hypnowheel is not registered.
   Rod looks.
1. **The banded renderer**, below. Profile Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel,
   and A/B every registered GL hack against the experiments branch with
   `tools/ab_flash.py`. Rod looks.
1. **Half resolution for Hypnowheel, as an option.** Render its GL frame at
   233 by 233 and scale up (as `hacks/lowrez_put.h` does for Fireworkx). Flash
   it and the full-resolution build pinned, and give Rod the numbers side by
   side; he chooses. Not for Unknown Pleasures, whose look is its thin lines.
1. **Whether Hypnowheel goes back into the rotation** is Rod's call after he
   has seen it.

### How a frame is drawn

- **Held frames.** A frame is held when it begins with a `glClear` of both the
  colour and the depth buffer (or of the colour buffer with the depth test
  off). From then until the swap, each triangle, line and point is transformed
  and lit as now and then stored, not drawn. A stored primitive keeps its
  screen-space vertices (`ZBufferPoint`, including the fractional line
  positions), its kind, and the state that affects rasterising: blend on and
  its function, depth test, depth write, polygon offset, shade model, smooth
  lines, and the dirty-box margin rule.
- **At the swap** (`glXSwapBuffers`, and any call that must see the pixels),
  the screen is drawn band by band. Each band starts in internal RAM as the
  clear colour and clear depth, gets every stored primitive that touches its
  rows, and is then copied to the canvas. Only rows inside the dirty box are
  copied; the dirty-box bookkeeping and the push are unchanged.
- **Fallback.** A frame draws straight to the canvas, as today, when it does
  not begin with such a clear (Pipes' incremental redraw), or when the store
  fills up. On overflow, the rest of the frame falls back. The builder may
  instead flush part-way, provided the result is correct.
- **Memory.** The bands and the store are allocated when a GL context opens
  and freed when it closes (`glshim_open`, and the release hook).
- **Inner loops.** The band rasteriser includes the two-pixel additive blend
  from issue #73 (a saturating RGB565 add with masks, two pixels per 32-bit
  word) and smooth lines that write to the band.

### Tests

- Banded frames compared with direct-drawn frames of the same scene on the
  host, within a small tolerance. The tolerance must be tight enough that a
  band seam, a missing band or a lost primitive fails.
- Exact tests for each fallback case: no clear, colour-only clear, store
  overflow.
- Tests for each state a stored primitive carries (blend, offset, depth test
  off, smooth lines), since each changes on the fly in Unknown Pleasures.
- Re-pin the frame hashes in `test_hacks.c` once the banded output is right,
  then check every GL hack on the board.

## Left to the builder

- Band height, from what fits in the internal RAM left over (probably 32 to
  64 rows), and whether bands are rows of the whole canvas or of the dirty box.
- The store's layout and size cap, and whether it lives in internal RAM or
  PSRAM (written once and read once per band, so sequential).
- How primitives are binned to bands (a list per band, or a sorted pass).
- How the rasterisers are limited to a band's rows: patching `ztriangle.h`'s
  row loop through `tinygl_patch.py`, or a `ZBuffer` whose `pbuf` and `zbuf`
  point at the band with a y offset.
- Whether points get their own fast path.
- Which calls besides the swap force the held frame out (`glFinish`,
  `glDrawPixels`, text drawing, a context change).

## Risks

- The estimate is rough. If rasterising in internal RAM costs a quarter of what
  it costs in PSRAM, Unknown Pleasures goes from 174 ms to roughly 80 ms and
  Hypnowheel, after its trig fix, to roughly 150 ms. Neither is measured.
- Triangle setup is repeated for each band a triangle touches. Hypnowheel's
  large triangles span many bands, and setup was already 61 ms.
- Unknown Pleasures switches between filled quads and lines with an offset
  within a frame, so a state-capture bug would show there first.

I've written the design to `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-banded-renderer-design.md` on a new branch, `feature/43-banded-renderer`. markdownlint passes.

The Agent tool's guidance is not to spawn subagents unless you ask, so I did the builder check myself, reading it as the person who has to build from it. One question came out that only you can answer, because it changes what gets built.

**Pipes and the z-buffer.** A banded frame keeps depth in internal RAM and throws it away after each band. Only colour goes back to the canvas. Pipes' incremental redraw clears once, then draws each new pipe segment against the depth left by earlier frames. So its first, banded frame would leave the PSRAM z-buffer out of date, and later segments would hide wrongly. The fallback alone doesn't cover this, because the damage is done by the frame before. 1. **Banded frames always write their depth back to PSRAM**, for the dirty rows only. It's automatic and fully one-path, but costs roughly 12 ms a frame on a full-screen hack like Unknown Pleasures. That's my estimate from the measured cache-miss cost.
2. **Pipes' wrapper turns banding off for itself.** That wrapper is our code, not the copied hack. It's free for every other hack, and it's a deliberate exception: Pipes is the only hack that builds on earlier frames.

I recommend option 2. Which do you want?

The calls I made myself, to check while you read:
- Bands and the holding area are allocated only while a GL context is open.
- A frame counts as cleared if it clears colour and depth, or clears colour with the depth test off. That covers HexTrail.
- When the holding area overflows, the rest of that frame falls back. The builder may flush part-way instead.
- The faster additive blend from #73 goes into the band rasteriser.
- Half resolution is for Hypnowheel only, and you choose after seeing both builds.
- Band height, the holding area's layout, and how the rasterisers are kept to a band's rows are left to whoever builds it.
